story: Li Yu was first author of the Atlas study YUX2010 in Nature. Working in rat kidney cells, the paper showed that mTOR is switched off when autophagy starts, then switches back on during long starvation. The renewed mTOR activity ends autophagy and drives autophagic lysosome reformation, where new lysosomes bud off from autolysosomes. The process was also seen in several animal species. PubMed lists Yu at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in Bethesda.

This was animal work, and it points to a mechanism rather than proving the same steps in depressed patients.

story: Sanjna Singh was first author of a 2026 trial in the Atlas, with Timothy J. Sargeant as a senior author. PubMed lists the author with the Lysosomal Health in Ageing group at the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute and at Adelaide University.

In a randomized crossover trial, 63 healthy adults ate a normal-protein diet and a reduced-protein diet for four weeks each. Autophagic flux in blood cells did not differ between the diets, even though animal work had suggested that less protein should raise autophagy.

studies.title: Reduced dietary protein intake does not alter autophagy in human blood: A randomized crossover study in healthy adults
studies.finding: In a rigorous randomized crossover trial, 63 healthy adults completed both a normal-protein (20% energy) and a reduced-protein (10% energy) diet for 4 weeks each. Despite preclinical evidence that dietary protein restriction should activate autophagy via mTORC1 inhibition, directly measured autophagic flux in blood immune cells did not change between the two diets. This is one of the few human studies to test the protein-restriction-to-autophagy link with a dynamic, flux-based (not just steady-state marker) readout, and the negative result suggests that moderate protein reduction alone, without an accompanying caloric deficit, is not sufficient to engage autophagy in humans the way it does i

story: Steven J Gamblin is the last author of a 2011 paper on the structure of AMPK, the cell's energy sensor that works against mTORC1 when energy is low. The work found that AMP binding protects AMPK from losing its activating phosphate, that ADP binding at one site gives the same protection without activating the enzyme, and it solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex.

PubMed gives an affiliation only for the first author in this record. The Mill Hill institute for Gamblin comes from a 2013 paper by the same team, where PubMed lists him at the MRC National Institute for Medical Research in London.

story: A 2021 study found that G3BP1 and G3BP2, proteins best known from stress granules, also hold the TSC complex on the lysosome. Without them, mTORC1 reacts too strongly to amino acids and insulin. A 2023 study showed that malonyl-CoA, a molecule made during fatty acid synthesis, binds the catalytic pocket of mTOR and blocks it, linking fat production to mTORC1 activity.
Brohee is a middle author on the 2021 paper and the second author on the 2023 paper. PubMed lists the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing in Cologne on both.

highlights.PRE2021: Middle author on the paper showing that G3BPs tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and restrain mTORC1.
highlights.NIC2023: Second of fourteen authors on the paper identifying malonyl-CoA as an ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor.

pubmed_affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing (MPI-AGE), Cologne, Germany.

studies.title: G3BPs tether the TSC complex to lysosomes and suppress mTORC1 signaling
studies.finding: Adds a physical brake upstream of mTORC1. G3BP1 and G3BP2, known until then as core stress-granule proteins, also sit on the cytoplasmic face of the lysosome and are what holds the TSC complex there; without them TSC cannot reach its target and mTORC1 becomes over-responsive to amino acids and insulin. Loss of G3BP1 reproduces TSC-like hyperactivity phenotypes: faster mTORC1-driven motility in breast cancer cells, with low G3BP1 correlating with worse patient outcome, and disturbed neuronal development in zebrafish. Relevant to the Atlas because it is a lysosomal tethering step that the canonical Rheb/TSC diagram does not show.

studies.title: Malonyl-CoA is a conserved endogenous ATP-competitive mTORC1 inhibitor
studies.finding: Malonyl-CoA, an intermediate of fatty-acid biosynthesis, binds the mTOR catalytic pocket directly and acts as a conserved ATP-competitive inhibitor of mTORC1; when fatty acid synthase is downregulated, rising malonyl-CoA feeds back to dampen mTORC1 activity, linking lipogenic capacity to overall biosynthetic output.

story: Alison M. Schram was first author of the 2025 phase 1 trial in the Atlas of RMC-5552, a drug built to block mTORC1 more than mTORC2. PubMed lists the author at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York.

The trial gave escalating weekly doses to 57 people with advanced solid tumours. High blood sugar, a side effect of older mTOR drugs, occurred in 4% of patients, and 64% had disease control. There was no comparison group and no head-to-head test against rapamycin, so this is early evidence.

highlights.SCH2025: First author of the phase 1 trial of RMC-5552 in advanced solid tumours.

pubmed_affiliation: Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, New York, New York

studies.title: The Bi-steric, mTORC1-Selective Inhibitor, RMC-5552, in Advanced Solid Tumors: A Phase 1 Trial
studies.finding: First-in-human, open-label dose-escalation trial (n=57, advanced solid tumors, no comparator arm) of a bi-steric mTORC1-selective inhibitor. Treatment-related hyperglycemia was low (4%) and not dose-limiting, alongside a 64% disease control rate. Because the trial was uncontrolled and made no head-to-head comparison against rapamycin or an ATP-site inhibitor, this is encouraging early clinical evidence consistent with the hypothesis that sparing mTORC2 reduces metabolic toxicity -- it does not establish mTORC2 sparing as the cause.

Lab experiments suggested that altered purines can impair mitochondria and promote microglial inflammation, but this was not tested in the patients. PubMed lists Roy at Simmaron Research and at the Milwaukee Institute for Drug Discovery.

Besides acting through TSC2, AMPK directly phosphorylates Raptor - the core mTORC1 subunit - to halt growth when energy runs low. studies.title: Efficacy and safety of everolimus for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (EXIST-1): a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial
studies.finding: Phase 3 RCT (n=117) in tuberous sclerosis, the disease where mTOR is stuck ON by a genetic fault. Everolimus shrank brain tumors (SEGA) by >=50% in 35% of patients versus 0% on placebo. Because the underlying cause here is direct mTOR overactivation, this is arguably the cleanest randomised human evidence that blocking mTOR works in a genetically defined mTORopathy -- which does not extend to mTOR inhibition in people without such a mutation.

story: Matthew D Demmings is first author of a 2026 paper in Cell Reports. In cell and animal models of Parkinson disease, long-lasting stress signaling through ATF4 turned up SESN2, DDIT4 and Trib3. Together these lowered both mTORC1 and mTORC2 activity, and that loss of mTOR signaling helped kill dopamine neurons through the protein PUMA. This is a case where too little mTOR activity is harmful. PubMed lists him at the University of Western Ontario.

highlights.DEMMINGS2026: First author of the study linking ATF4-driven mTOR suppression to dopaminergic neuron death in Parkinson disease models.

pubmed_affiliation: Neuroscience Program, University of Western Ontario, London, ON, Canada; Robarts Research Institute, University of Western Ontario, London, ON, Canada.

studies.title: ATF4 activates a transcriptional program that chronically suppresses mTOR activity and promotes neurodegeneration in Parkinson disease models
studies.finding: Chronic integrated-stress-response signalling through ATF4 coordinately upregulates SESN2, DDIT4 and Trib3, which together suppress BOTH mTORC1 and mTORC2; this sustained mTOR inhibition drives dopaminergic neuron death via the pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family protein PUMA. Defines a maladaptive ISR/ATF4-to-mTOR axis in Parkinson disease models — a case where LESS mTOR activity is harmful, opposite to the usual longevity framing.

current.lab_name: Newcastle University Institute for Ageing, Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences, Newcastle University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
current.role: First author of a 2018 mouse study of rapamycin in mice with enhanced NF-kB activity.
current.sub: Newcastle University Institute for Ageing, Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences
story: Clara Correia-Melo was first author of a 2018 paper in Aging Cell. PubMed lists the author at the Newcastle University Institute for Ageing and the Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences at Newcastle University.

The team gave rapamycin to mice with genetically raised NF-kB activity, which develop low-grade inflammation and age early. Rapamycin did not lengthen life or reduce inflammation. It did reduce frailty and improved memory, coordination and tissue structure, and senescence markers fell. The result suggests that healthspan benefits of rapamycin can be separate from its anti-inflammatory effect, at least in these mice.

highlights.COR2018: First author of the mouse study showing rapamycin improved healthspan without reducing inflammaging in nfkb1-null mice.

pubmed_affiliation: Newcastle University Institute for Ageing, Institute for Cell and Molecular Biosciences, Newcastle University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK.

studies.title: Rapamycin improves healthspan but not inflammaging in nfκb1(-/-) mice.
studies.finding: Separates two effects of rapamycin that are usually assumed to travel together. In mice with genetically enhanced NF-kB activity, rapamycin showed no benefit in lifespan and no reduction of inflammaging, yet still reduced frailty and improved long-term memory, neuromuscular coordination and tissue architecture, with lower markers of cellular senescence. Healthspan benefit is therefore uncoupled here from suppression of inflammation, which is a boundary condition on the common claim that rapamycin acts on ageing mainly by damping inflammation. Note the mixed result: the healthspan outcomes are positive, the lifespan and inflammaging outcomes are null.

current.lab_name: Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research (Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA)
current.role: Co-author of two Novartis trials of mTOR inhibitors given to older adults to see if immune function improves.
current.sub: Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research, Cambridge, MA · listed on two Atlas papers, 2014 and 2018
story: David J. Glass is a middle author on two human trials in the Atlas, both from Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Both asked whether a short, low-dose course of an mTOR inhibitor can help the aging immune system.

In the 2014 study, older volunteers took everolimus before a flu shot and their antibody response rose by about 20 percent. In the 2018 phase 2a trial of 264 older adults, a low-dose combination of two mTOR inhibitors was linked to fewer reported infections over the next year. A later, larger trial of one of the drugs did not confirm a clinical benefit. Two 2001 muscle papers in the Atlas list a D J Glass, but PubMed gives only initials there, so they are not covered here.

highlights.MAN2014: Middle author of the trial showing that everolimus raised the flu-vaccine response by about 20 percent in older volunteers.
highlights.MAN2018: Middle author of the phase 2a trial linking low-dose TORC1 inhibition to fewer infections in 264 older adults.

pubmed_affiliation: Novartis Institutes for Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA.

studies.title: mTOR inhibition improves immune function in the elderly
studies.finding:
Older volunteers took the rapalog everolimus (RAD001) before a flu shot, and their antibody response to the vaccine rose by about 20% at doses that were fairly well tolerated. The share of T cells carrying the exhaustion marker PD-1 also fell. The PEARL authors summarise the doses as 0.5 mg daily or 5 mg weekly for 6 weeks. This is the human result behind the weekly low-dose idea.
Boundary: a stronger vaccine response is a lab marker, not fewer infections, and the later RTB101 trial (MAN2021) shows how that gap can matter.

studies.title: TORC1 inhibition enhances immune function and reduces infections in the elderly
studies.finding: A phase 2a RCT in 264 older adults: 6 weeks of a low-dose combination of BEZ235 (a catalytic PI3K/mTOR inhibitor) and everolimus (RAD001) was associated with fewer reported infections over the following year, plus higher antiviral gene expression and a better flu-vaccine response. The later phase 3 trial of RTB101 (BEZ235) alone (MAN2021) did not confirm a clinical benefit.
